title: Febrile seizures, status epilepticus and epilepsy care
blurb: Keep a seizing child safe, recognise convulsive status epilepticus at 5 minutes, give first and second-line treatment under NICE NG217, and advise families after a febrile seizure.
question: Oscar, 6, is having a convulsive seizure on the children's ward that has now lasted 5 minutes. He has a working IV cannula and resuscitation equipment is at hand. He has no individual emergency plan. What should be given?

teach.body: A seizure is a sudden burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. A febrile seizure happens with a high temperature in a child aged usually 6 months to 6 years, with no other cause; it usually lasts 2 to 3 minutes and is not epilepsy. Epilepsy is a tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures. Convulsive status epilepticus is a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more. Plain English: time every seizure, keep the child safe, and treat at 5 minutes.
teach.cite: NICE NG217 (updated Aug 2026); NHS Febrile seizures

items: Note the time the seizure starts and ends.
Protect the head with your hands or something soft; move dangerous objects away.
Do not restrain the child or put anything in their mouth.
Give oxygen and monitor in hospital; check blood glucose.
Afterwards, place the child in the recovery position and check the airway is clear.

steps.label: Plan available?
steps.sub: Give medication as written in the child's emergency plan

steps.label: No plan
steps.sub: Buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam; IV lorazepam if IV access and resus facilities

steps.label: 5–10 min later
steps.sub: Second benzodiazepine dose; 999 in the community

steps.label: Still seizing
steps.sub: IV levetiracetam, phenytoin or sodium valproate

teach.caption: Look for causes such as hypoglycaemia. NG217 notes levetiracetam may be quicker to give with fewer adverse effects.

after first benzodiazepine: give a second
drowsiness beyond this after a febrile seizure: 999

head: Feature
rows: Stiffness or twitching on one side only
More sleepy than usual for over 1 hour afterwards
teach.caption: A child who has had a first febrile seizure needs to be checked in hospital, to look for the cause of the fever.

teach.text: Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures. Give paracetamol or ibuprofen for distress, not to stop a seizure happening, and do not sponge or strip a feverish child. Parents often blame themselves for 'not getting the temperature down'.

teach.body: Agree an individualised emergency management plan after convulsive status epilepticus or repeated (cluster) seizures if there is concern they may recur, so that school staff and parents can give rescue medication such as buccal midazolam. Repeated or cluster seizures (typically 3 or more self-terminating seizures in 24 hours) are a medical emergency. Sodium valproate must not be started in under-55s unless two specialists document there is no alternative, and girls who could become pregnant need the Pregnancy Prevention Programme.
teach.cite: NICE NG217 recs 7.1.12, 7.2.1, 7.2.4 and box 2; MHRA valproate measures

teach.body: Aisha has epilepsy and starts a tonic-clonic seizure in class. The school nurse times it, cushions her head and clears the area. At 5 minutes she gives buccal midazolam exactly as written in Aisha's emergency management plan, and calls 999 as the plan instructs. When the seizure stops, she puts Aisha in the recovery position, stays with her and records the times and what was given for the ambulance crew.

teach.caption: Children who have had a febrile seizure have only a slightly increased chance of epilepsy later.

items: Convulsive status epilepticus = seizure lasting 5 minutes or more.
First line: the child's emergency plan; otherwise buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam, or IV lorazepam with IV access and resus facilities.
Second benzodiazepine after 5–10 minutes; then IV levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate.
Check glucose; do not restrain or put anything in the mouth; recovery position afterwards.
Febrile seizures: usually 6 months–6 years, 2–3 minutes; antipyretics do not prevent them.

summary: You can now keep a seizing child safe, recognise status epilepticus at 5 minutes and give first and second-line treatment in line with NG217. You can also tell febrile seizures from epilepsy and advise parents when to call 999.

A.q: Oscar, 6, has had a convulsive seizure on the ward for 5 minutes. He has a working IV cannula and resuscitation equipment is ready. He has no emergency plan. What should be given?
A.why: NG217 rec 7.1.3: with IV access and resuscitation facilities immediately available, give IV lorazepam as first-line treatment.

whyNot.0: Levetiracetam is second line after 2 benzodiazepine doses.
whyNot.3: Phenytoin is a second-line option after benzodiazepines.

A.q: Ben, 7, starts a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the playroom. What should the nurse do first?
options: Hold his arms to stop injury
Sit him upright in a chair
Put a padded spatula between his teeth
Note the time and protect his head
A.why: Time the seizure, protect the head and move hazards away. Do not restrain or put anything in the mouth.

whyNot.0: Restraining a seizing child can cause injury.
whyNot.1: Moving him into a chair risks a fall and airway problems.
whyNot.2: Nothing should be put in the mouth during a seizure.

A.q: Leo, 2, is going home after his first febrile seizure. His father asks whether giving paracetamol and ibuprofen at the first sign of fever will stop another. What is the best answer?
options: Yes, if both are given together
Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures
Ibuprofen prevents them; paracetamol does not
A.why: Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures (NG143; NHS). They can be used for distress.

whyNot.0: Giving both together is not advised and does not prevent seizures.
whyNot.1: Regular dosing does not prevent febrile seizures.
whyNot.3: Neither ibuprofen nor paracetamol prevents febrile seizures.

B.q: Zara, 4, has been fitting for 12 minutes at nursery. Buccal midazolam was given at 5 minutes from her plan, and the seizure has not stopped. An ambulance has been called. What does NG217 recommend next?
options: A second dose of benzodiazepine as per her plan
Wait for the paramedics without further treatment
Cold sponging to lower her temperature
B.why: NG217 rec 7.1.8: follow the emergency plan or give a second benzodiazepine dose if the seizure does not stop within 5 to 10 minutes of the first.

whyNot.1: A second dose is recommended at 5 to 10 minutes after the first.
whyNot.2: IV second-line drugs are given in hospital after 2 benzodiazepine doses.
whyNot.3: Sponging is not recommended and does not stop a seizure.

B.q: Ethan, 10, with type 1 diabetes, has a generalised seizure that stops after 3 minutes. He is in the recovery position. What is the priority check?
B.why: Hypoglycaemia is a key treatable cause of seizures, especially in a child with diabetes; check glucose straight away.

whyNot.1: Peak flow is not relevant after a seizure.
whyNot.2: Urine testing does not identify an immediate treatable cause.
whyNot.3: Bilateral BP is not the priority after a seizure in a child with diabetes.

B.q: Maya, 18 months, had a febrile seizure lasting 2 minutes. An hour and a half later she remains much sleepier than usual. What should the nurse advise?
options: This is expected; let her sleep
Book a GP appointment for tomorrow
B.why: NHS advice: call 999 if the child is more sleepy than usual for more than 1 hour after the seizure.

whyNot.0: Drowsiness beyond 1 hour is a warning sign, not expected.
whyNot.1: Paracetamol does not address prolonged drowsiness.
whyNot.3: Waiting until tomorrow delays urgent assessment.

C.q: Jamie, 11, has had two doses of benzodiazepine on the ward but is still in convulsive status epilepticus. Which is a second-line option in NG217?
C.why: NG217 rec 7.1.9: if status does not respond to 2 benzodiazepine doses, give IV levetiracetam, phenytoin or sodium valproate.

whyNot.0: NG217 moves to second-line drugs after 2 benzodiazepine doses.
whyNot.1: Adrenaline is for anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest, not seizures.
whyNot.2: Oral medicines are not used in status epilepticus.

C.q: Sophie, 14, has epilepsy and her consultant is considering sodium valproate. What safety measure applies?
options: It can be started by any doctor in clinic
It is the preferred choice for girls over 12
No contraception advice is needed for her
C.why: MHRA/NG217: valproate must not be started in under-55s unless two specialists independently document that there is no other effective or tolerated treatment; the Pregnancy Prevention Programme applies.

whyNot.0: Starting valproate requires two specialists to document it is the only option.
whyNot.2: Valproate is avoided where possible in girls who could become pregnant.
whyNot.3: The Pregnancy Prevention Programme includes contraception.

C.q: Aisha, 9, has epilepsy. Her seizure at school reaches 5 minutes. Her emergency management plan is in her bag. What should the school nurse do?
options: Give rectal diazepam from the first aid box
Give medication as written in her plan
Call her parents for permission first
C.why: NG217 rec 7.1.2: if an individualised emergency management plan is immediately available, give medication as detailed in the plan.

whyNot.0: The child's own plan takes priority over a general choice.
whyNot.3: Seeking permission delays emergency treatment already agreed in the plan.

reteach.title: The 5-minute rule
reteach.question: What happens at the 5-minute mark of a convulsive seizure, and what comes next?

blocks.body: Most seizures stop by themselves within a few minutes. Once a convulsive seizure reaches 5 minutes it is status epilepticus and needs treatment: the child's plan, or buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam (IV lorazepam in hospital). If it carries on 5 to 10 minutes after that dose, give a second dose. If two doses fail, move to an IV second-line drug.

blocks.text: Do not wait for a seizure to 'run its course' past 5 minutes: the longer it lasts, the harder it is to stop.

explain.body: Time it, protect the head, remove hazards, do not restrain, nothing in the mouth, recovery position afterwards, check the airway.

rows.label: After
values: Give food or drink at once

test.q: What should be done once a seizure has stopped?
options: Give a small drink of water straight away
Cold sponge to cool them down
Sit the child upright so they can talk
test.why: After the seizure, place the child in the recovery position and make sure nothing is obstructing the mouth or throat.

whyNot.2: A post-ictal child should lie in the recovery position, not sit up.

explain.body: At 5 minutes: emergency plan, or buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam in the community, or IV lorazepam with IV access and resuscitation facilities.

test.q: A child with no plan has a 5-minute seizure in a park. Paramedics are not yet there. Which treatment is first line?
test.why: In the community without IV access, give buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam.

whyNot.0: IV lorazepam needs IV access and resuscitation facilities.
whyNot.2: Oral tablets cannot be given safely during a seizure.
whyNot.3: Phenytoin is a second-line IV drug.

explain.body: Second benzodiazepine dose if the seizure continues 5 to 10 minutes after the first. If 2 doses fail: IV levetiracetam, phenytoin or sodium valproate.

test.q: How long after the first benzodiazepine should a second dose be given if the seizure continues?
test.why: NG217 rec 7.1.8: give a second dose if the seizure does not stop within 5 to 10 minutes of the first.

whyNot.0: 1 to 2 minutes is too soon for the drug to act.
whyNot.1: 30 minutes is far too long to wait.
whyNot.3: An hour would leave status untreated.

explain.body: Usually 6 months to 6 years, 2 to 3 minutes. 999 if first seizure, over 5 minutes, breathing difficulty, one-sided, sleepy over 1 hour, or more than 1 in 24 hours. Antipyretics do not prevent them.

test.q: Which feature after a febrile seizure should prompt a 999 call?
test.why: Stiffness or twitching on only one side of the body is a reason to call 999.

whyNot.1: Fever is the usual trigger, not itself a 999 criterion.
whyNot.2: Crying shows the child is responsive.
